utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. I understand, Mr. Vasic, there may be some unhappy news?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everybody in the courtroom. Unfortunately, Your Honours, we have bad news. Yesterday we mentioned the medical condition of my client, and the information I conveyed to you yesterday is not complete or fully accurate. In the meantime I had the opportunity to see my client at the hospital and I must say that there was no regular examination performed on him, that that's what he said to me in person, and I would prefer to give you the other details in a private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, Mr. Vasic, we understand from you that your client is undergoing some further tests at Bronovo Hospital today and we will await the results of those with interest and concern, but in the meantime your client has indicated his agreement to the evidence of the present witness continuing, in his absence. Yes. Thank you very much for that. If the witness could be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. May I remind you of the affirmation --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- which still applies. Now, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Danilovic.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: We'll now continue to hear you where we stopped yesterday, and that's why I would ask for document 65 ter to be put on the screen. The reference number is 1D07 and ERN number 0D000511. That's the report of the wounding of the commander of TO Vukovar that we started discussing yesterday, but we stopped because our time had elapsed. This document is part of the set of documents. It's the sixth in the sequence, under --

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Tell me, in what capacity did the Colonel Vojnovic report to the commander of the motor district about the wounding of the commander of TO Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that as a town commander of Vukovar, he was required to report to the superior command about this grave incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Please read to us the first sentence from this report.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "On December 4th, 1991, in the Velepromet building in Vukovar where the TO Vukovar is stationed", well this is not the exact formulation as it should be -- "while returning to an official task to sheet [as interpreted] the commander of TO Vukovar Miroljub Vojnovic was wounded by his personal escort Goran Covic".

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Danilovic. We needn't go on.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But this should read the Chief of Staff of TO Vukovar. This is not phrased the way it should have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, but I would like to know something else. The staff of TO Vukovar was located at Velepromet. Are you acquainted with this fact?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The staff of the TO of Vukovar was located at Velepromet, and all persons to be identified were sent to the staff, which was located at Velepromet, because the staff, who were locals, knew most people from the area, and that was the main reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: With Exhibit number 781, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yesterday we spoke about the order of the commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade to relocate the command of the unit to the barracks, and your role in that process. I now suggest that Exhibit 444 be put on the screen. Thank you. Perhaps we could zoom in on the first half. Mr. Danilovic, you will not find this document in the set you are looking at, so please look at the screen in front of you. Please take a look at this order and read to us the letterhead and what does this order represent. Wait for the interpretation to finish, please.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an order of the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade dated November 22nd, 1991 about the regulation of the establishment of military authority and the -- providing security for the units and the command in the town of Vukovar and the wider surroundings, actually in the area of responsibility of the 80th brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Kindly read to us the first paragraph of this order.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 1 of this order reads that: "The relocation of the unit into the Vukovar barracks is being ordered. The 80th company of military police, the 80th company of communication, the 80th platoon of ABHO and the 80th command -- 80th command as well as the brigade command on November 22nd should be relocated there. Accommodation shall be provided for the units, and duty as well as security shall be organised. "Under the conditions of permanent readiness, to be able to react to attacks on military and other buildings of special significance in order to organise functional military authority". This is the content of item 1 of this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Apart from this relocation of this command to the Vukovar barracks, is the second part, the organisation of security, in any relation with what you told us yesterday about attacks on some units by remaining forces of the ZNG and the MUP?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, and I think I remember well, between the 15th and the 18th of November, a complete -- the complete command of a unit was massacred because there was no adequate security provided. I remember that until December 6th or 7th there were instances of members of the ZNG and the MUP of Croatia were pulling out from hidden shelters and we know that in the town of Vukovar there were many underground catacombs, so to speak, where they were hiding. And there was constant danger that some of the units or commands as well as the population, although there was little population left in the town, so there was constant danger of them being at risk, and that's why these measures were ordered, and based on the order of the command of the first motorised district and the command of OG South, that were in force at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You spoke at more length about the relations with the motor district and OG South, but let us now take a look at item 2.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 2 of this order reads: "The staff of TO Vukovar in cooperation with the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade shall organise the establishment of authorities in local communities, so that they are functional, organise the manner of movement of the population returning to town --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Excuse me a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt my learned friend. We've been trying to get it in English. We don't have the electronic version in English at all. We only have it in B/C/S. I don't know why that should be, because clearly the Court has got it in English. And when I go on to e-court, I've only got it in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I can help, Your Honours. My reference is ERN 0D000531 -- 39, that is the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The problem seems to be resolved, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. We can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Danilovic, please read item 2 once more, as slowly as the first time round.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So item 2: "The staff of TO Vukovar in cooperation with the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade will organise the establishment of functional authority in local communities, organise police stations, regulate the manner of movement of the population returning to town, and the mandatory identification at the Velepromet centre". This is the complete content of item 2 of this order of the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: We're speaking about mandatory identification at the Velepromet centre. Was that the identification that you mentioned a little while ago while we were speaking about the wounding of Miroljub Vujovic?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please read out item 3 of this order.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 3. "The staff of the TO Vukovar shall be deployed at a more adequate site in the vicinity of the Vukovar barracks, according to the decision of commander Miroljub Vujovic".

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: This reads: Commander Miroljub Vujovic. They didn't say commander of what?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of -- the commander or rather the Chief of Staff of TO Vukovar I suppose it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Kindly read out to us item five.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item five of this order reads: "The staff of TO Vukovar in cooperation with the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade will prevent all sorts of theft and misuse of property in the town of Vukovar and the surrounding villages".

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the relationship was between the staff of TO Vukovar and the command of the 80th brigade, bearing in mind the fact that they are working on the same task and this reads, in cooperation with. What kind of cooperation was that, and how did they cooperate on those tasks in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The staff of TO Vukovar, in military terms, was not subordinate to the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade. This is why the order reads "in cooperation". So there was two-way cooperation between the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade and the staff of TO Vukovar. So this was two-way cooperation, and it had to do with the tasks mentioned in this order, and in other documents that defined other tasks and authorities and the commander coordinated certain tasks with the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Danilovic. Please now read out item 7.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 7 of this order reads: "The necessary coordination of the rehabilitation of the theatre shall be regulated by the command of OG South in cooperation with the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade, and the staff of TO Vukovar".

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Hereto, the word "cooperation" is mentioned. Can you tell us about the relations between OG South, the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade and the staff of TO Vukovar as we're talking about cooperation.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is obvious from this order that the command of OG South has the responsibility to rehabilitate the theatre and this shall be done in cooperation with the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade and the staff of TO Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was that after -- after handover?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that this was at the very junction when the command of the brigade was no longer part of OG South, and that's why this reads "cooperation". Otherwise the command of OG South would have given out orders rather than cooperating.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will no longer need this exhibit. I would now go back -- or discuss the following events. Do you know that in early December in Vukovar a civilian authority was established? Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I think that Babic or what his name was was the president of the executive council, but I cannot tell for sure. I know that the establishment of a civilian authorities had begun, and the command of the first motor district made efforts to assist them, also by sending some officers over from Belgrade. As for the exact date of the establishment of civilian authority, I really don't remember what date it was. It's been a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You did say something about that yesterday, and we'll not be requiring a specific date. If you can't remember. I would like to go back to that mission you had on the 18th of November, as commander of that collection camp for POWs at Ovcara, those were being brought over from Mitnica. I would like to see Exhibit 432 please, more specifically, page 48 and page 49. This document is already an exhibit. This is the working notebook of Captain Vezmarovic, the commander of the military police company of the 80th Motorised Brigade. Pages 48 and 49, please. Mr. Danilovic, on the right hand side you see a list starting with Filip Karaula and then it goes on. We look at the following pages -- if we could just turn the page, please, and have a look at another couple of pages, number 50, 51, 52, 53. This is a list which Captain Vezmarovic claims he drew up himself, a list of the captured members of the MUP and ZNG who had been brought over from Mitnica and who were guarded on the 18th and the morning of the 19th at the Ovcara farm. Are you aware of a list like this being drawn up by Captain Vezmarovic?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be quite honest, I can't remember whether indeed he drew up a list like that, or not. But he probably did. I can't say I noticed him doing that in all honesty. I couldn't say. I suppose he did make a list. It is obvious he --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Could I just object, because it's happened a number of times that the witness himself says he doesn't know, and that he's guessing on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It sounds conjectural, Mr. Vasic, just the witness trying to see what he suggests is an explanation for the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am asking the witness about this document and he'll tell us what he remembers, and what he does not remember, what he knows and what he does not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: He says he doesn't remember, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He says he doesn't remember the list. I agree. I will refrain from showing him the list any more, since he doesn't seem to remember this list, or rather, he said he didn't remember Captain Vezmarovic drawing up a list, but perhaps I can ask the witness the following question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was there any order to draw up a list of POWs?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, an order came to make a list, for us to know exactly who the POWs were. There was an order like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: But you don't know who made the lists or when?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's really difficult for me to say. It has been a very long time, and I would be hard put to remember the exact time when lists were made, in terms of hours and minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could we please go to page 63 now. It's not about the list. It's about something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I tried to indicate to my learned friend that I did object to that course, if this witness doesn't know that this man has made the list, how can he be referred to the content? All it is is analogous to leading the witness, at the very least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have moved on, Mr. Moore. I'm sorry, you're still wanting the witness to look at some part of this list, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. This is in fact no longer a list. This is a note about the handover of POWs, or rather, their surrender. I want to know whether the witness remembers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Moore is objecting to the procedure of showing the witness a document and then asking for his comments. As you know, the normal procedure would be to ask the witness about events. And if the witness, in his recollection, recalls a list or recalls a note or is then able to identify a note as being what he was talking about, the document becomes admissible. It's going to be slower, but Mr. Moore is putting that objection, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, Your Honour, but the document under consideration now is already exhibited. This is a Captain Vezmarovic exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is not a matter of exhibiting the document. It's a matter of whether the witness knows anything about the document or what is recorded in it, and that should be his own oral evidence, not prompted by what somebody may have written in some document at some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Your Honour. I'll first ask the witness and then we'll see what happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Danilovic, you were the commander of this facility on the 18th and 19th of November.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who brought these people from Mitnica to your facility, the facility under your command and control? And who did you surrender these people to?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ZNG/MUP POWs were brought to the camp by a security detail led by an officer, whose name simply escapes me. We put the prisoners up in a building at the Ovcara farm where security was provided. From the afternoon of the 18th through the following night to the 19th, at some point in the morning when they were transferred to Sremska Mitrovica for further procedure. Now which officer it was who brought them there with the security detail escorting them, I really can't remember the officer's name.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if they were surrendered to that same officer on their way to Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was there an officer to whom you surrendered these POWs when they were being taken to Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. We couldn't just leave them to the security people. There had to be someone to officially take charge of them and escort them to the collection centre in Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I would like to show you, now, what Captain Vezmarovic noted down about the surrender of these prisoners or about their handover, to see if that can jog your memory, and that's what I have on page 63. It's about the officer you mentioned. "Received on the 18th of November, 1991 at around 1600 hours at the Ovcara farm. Handed over to Captain Karanfilov. On the 19th of November at about 11.30 hours. List submitted to the Sremska Mitrovica KPD on the 19th of November at about 1530 hours". What about this entry? Does that perhaps ring a bell? Do you remember that, the officer mentioned here, this Captain?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that it was almost certainly him, but I couldn't remember his name. It has been an awfully long time and many things happened, too many things in fact for me to keep track of every single person that appeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Who brought these lists to Sremska Mitrovica? Is this something you remember? Was it actually Captain Vezmarovic who physically took the lists as far as Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it might have been him, but I really can't say with any degree of certainty whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us yesterday that in your capacity as Chief of Staff, while you were away, you later familiarised yourself with the entries to the operations log as to what happened while you were away, because one of your duties was to check the operations, the war log, right?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can we just please have Exhibit 371, the entry for the 20th of November at 1600 hours. For the benefit of my learned friends, the English reference is page 11. We can have the English brought up on our monitors, since the witness has a B/C/S copy available. Mr. Danilovic, have you found that?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What exactly did you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The 20th of November, 1600 hours.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can I ask you to please read what it says there, and tell us what it means.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It reads: "The brigade commander has requested that shifts of officers be assigned for guarding the captured ZNG and MUP members. A military police platoon will be responsible for this, as well as the officers from the brigade command". It's a poor copy of the handwriting. It's not readily legible. This was actually an assignment that was handed out by the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Doesn't the same thing apply as to when you were the security commander, the same units were used, the military police platoon and the brigade command officers, right?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can't really be that specific. There may have been someone from the reconnaissance company involved in the security regime on the 18th of November when I was a POW camp commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I object again. Pure speculation. The witness has given evidence that he wasn't at Ovcara on that day. He is using phrases that it may have been, and it's exactly the same objection that I lodged earlier on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Vasic, it is an objectionable way of obtaining evidence. The issue is whether this witness remembers anything about these events. And on the face of it at the moment, he does not.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was asking, based on this entry, about the units that were used. I didn't ask the witness whether he was there on the 20th. I just wanted to check whether he saw the same units being used in the operations log, and then asked him whether these were the same units he had used on the 18th based on the entries in the operations log, but I will stop this line of questions so we can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Danilovic, what sort of reputation did Captain first class commander of the LAD PVO of the 80th Brigade enjoy with his soldiers?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is with full responsibility that I can now tell you that the commander of the LAD PVO of the 80th Motorised Brigade was a highly trained officer held in high esteem by his soldiers, and well liked too. They trusted him in every way, ranging from his military training and ability to any other quality that might be desirable in a military commander. He enjoyed a particularly high reputation in his own unit, and in his work with the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of any problems that he had since he's known to be a non-Serb and joined the division just before the departure for Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing that I'd be familiar with. Nothing that I'd know of. It is quite evident, however, that he was the one who got the division mobilised, who brought it into the deployment area of the brigade, and that he was involved in combat operations throughout. I can't be specific. There may have been random individual incidents, someone saying something, but nothing that could possibly have affected his work as an officer or could have kept him from performing his tasks, establishment wise.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Danilovic. I'll ask you some questions to do with the rules that applied in your unit. What about the security organs in your unit, did they hand out orders to military police units that were there?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of security of the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade was authorised to issue certain orders directly to the military police company commander. No doubt about that. And the same thing applied to the brigade commander, or the Chief of Staff in his absence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You referred here to the commander's absence. You were Chief of Staff of the 80th Brigade, right? What were the situations in which you were authorised to sign orders on behalf of your commander? Give us an example, please.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A Chief of Staff in any command only ever signs documents or orders when the brigade commander is absent. If he's at a forward command post or anywhere outside his original command post, then the Chief of Staff has the responsibility of signing documents and orders in the commander's absence. And this is in keeping with the combat rules for all units.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, you say that he exercises command over a unit when the commander himself is absent. He acts as some sort of a deputy, right?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is very much so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Danilovic. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this concludes my examination-in-chief of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic. Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would seem that I have several questions for this witness, since I've got my lectern up and all the questions prepared. So if I may have a go, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, as a special privilege, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Danilovic, good morning. I'm Milan Lukic, one of Mr. Sljivancanin's Defence counsel. I would like to ask you a number of questions now stemming from the answers you provided to Mr. Vasic. I'll mostly be addressing the subjects that you have already discussed.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The same thing applies as before. Please hold a little after each of my questions so as to avoid any overlaps between questions and answers. Question number 1. Can you tell me about the similarities and differences between an operations log and a war log, in a brigade? You appear to be familiar with the way these documents are kept and produced.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There certainly is some degree of difference between the two. The name itself, a war log, implies that this is one of the paramount documents in any command. The kind of document kept in wartime is combat operations, are conducted entries are made to the war log recording the most important developments over a 24-hour period in an area of combat operations. An operations log is more of a peacetime thing, it's kept in peacetime. Normally it records the situation that prevails at a certain time in a unit. And this would be the essential difference between the two. Now, why were both logs kept? I don't think that is a relevant issue right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's not something that I necessarily want to know about. Perhaps the OTP might. You have looked at both documents during your proofing and during your preparation for this testimony. I'm talking about the operations log and the war log of your own brigade. We agree, if I put it to you that in relation to the security regime at Ovcara and what went on there, in terms of putting up prisoners, their detention, there's a lot more information in the operations log in relation to that than in the war log, if you look at all the information that both documents bring. Or rather, this information in relation to this matter primarily entered into the operations log as opposed to the war log.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite obviously entries should have been made to both logs. However, the operations duty officers of the brigade command, depending on whose shift it was, did what they did and kept the logs this way. Sometimes -- not all information was recorded in great detail, but sometimes even the nitty-gritty was provided in specific cases. As far as Ovcara was concerned, both sorts of entries should have been made just to keep it identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But there's actually more information to be found in the operations log?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it comes across. That's how it turned out and that much is obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll ask you several questions regarding the military police company, what Mr. Vasic asked you near the end of his examination-in-chief. The evidence that we have heard suggests that the military police company remained attached to the command throughout its time in Vukovar and that it was a staff unit for all practical intents throughout the fighting in Vukovar. The military police company led by Mr. Vezmarnovic. Would you agree with what I'm putting to you? This is merely evidence that we have heard in this trial.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You looked at the operations log twice yesterday and I'm not asking for that to be read out again, but I would just like to remind you that 14th of November entry at about 1700 hours, the 15th of November, 1700 hours, daily combat reports recorded in the operations log in both cases we have references there; two reports by the military police company. What exactly do you know about those daily combat reports? Were they regular and who were they submitted to?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Daily combat reports were submitted by all the brigade command units, including the staff units, including the military police company. These were received at the operation centre of the brigade command, and it is the duty operations officer who receives all of these in order to draft a regular combat report which, in turn, is signed by the brigade commander and submitted by the brigade commander to the superior command. This is a document about the overall combat readiness of a unit on a given day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As far as I understand, these reports were submitted on a daily basis by 1700 hours, right?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know if these reports continued to be submitted at the time the brigade moved to Vukovar and, for all practical intents, became the town command?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the practice continued. Reports were still being sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: A little while ago Mr. Vasic said to you about -- asked you about who was authorised to pass orders to the commander of the motor police. My question is whether the security element was authorised to give orders to the commander of the company of the motor police or only if authorised to do so by the commander.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is usual practice for the commander to give authority to the commander of security, to give authority to the commander of the military police, since he is best acquainted with the capabilities of the military police, and thus best able to employ them as a staff unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You have also said already, and I will repeat what we have heard already, you, as Chief of Staff, that's how I interpret your testimony --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Could I just.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- were authorised to pass orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm concerned about an entry on 2123, and it has an importance for the case, clearly. I read, in the English: "It is usual practice for the commander to give authority to the commander of security, to give authority to the commander". Our understanding would be, is that it is orders, and not authority. And I see Mr. Lukic nodding in agreement with that. And there is an important distinction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You are content that the word is appropriately "orders", are you, Mr. Lukic? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't want to discuss this issue with the witness or to produce evidence, but the question was: Can the security element give orders? I'm not speaking about control of the motorised police, but can the security element at the brigade, the motorised infantry brigade give orders to the motor police only if authorised to do so by the commander? So if they have a special authority to do so, that is what I mean.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I said a minute ago that certain authorities for their employment, but that is regulated by the rules that are in force for the motor police, what the security element can do, what kind of orders they can pass, if authorised by the commander. This is usual practice and has never been a problem and we didn't have any problems with that while we were attacking Vukovar, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me simplify some more. You know that there are rules of service pertaining to the activities of the military police and the security element. Do you know whether, at the time, these rules were adhered to in your brigade?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were adhered to the way it is regulated by rules of engagement for the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you, as Chief of Staff, at any time -- we're talking now about the time when your brigade was around Vukovar -- pass out orders to the commander of the military police company without prior authority received from commander Vojnovic?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever the commander was absent, I gave orders to the commander of the military police, but while the commander of the brigade was present, it was not necessary. Only if the commander was extremely busy, I consulted him whether I could give orders to the military police, to perform some duties from his responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So only after prior consultation with the commander?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So this refers to the testimony about that -- that was on page 8829, reference number 15/5. You testified about your departure on the mission at Nemci village. So you left on the 20th in the morning and returned on the 21st. Do you know -- I will first ask you if any soldier is killed on that day in your unit? Is it necessary to report about that to the superior command if the death of a soldier is established and his identity is known?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. At the same moment. As soon as possible a report about an extraordinary event in the unit is made. That's what we did and there have been no problems with that. This was also the case with soldiers being wounded or committing suicide or leaving the unit. This was all reported and this was also put in the combat report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If the military police must conduct an on-site investigation, this is probably also reported, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A report is produced, only -- as far as I remember some reports followed the security line. They did not follow the line of command. That was what the rules said too. But in the case of woundings, et cetera, this followed the command line. But certain reports followed the security line toward the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that Captain Vezmarovic, on the 19th or 20th, performed an on-site investigation in Sotin. Do you remember anything about that? If you do, all right. If you don't, well ...

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember little. One or two soldiers from the pioneer regiment were killed while clearing the area. I cannot remember anything more, because it's been too long a time. So I cannot confirm who was where, and at what time and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sir, please take another look at Exhibit 371. The entry dated 18th November, 14 hours 30 minutes. Mr. Vasic has already read this out to you, so I won't repeat that. The operations log.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a minute. On the 18th?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. At 14 hours 10 minutes. This says that everybody had left to the Ovcara farm and the task was to establish a camp to admit captured members of the ZNG and MUP from the Mitnica area.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you said about the following item that you had been appointed as commander of that camp.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And on the following day, as has been said, at 1200 hours, they were handed over and taken to Sremska Mitrovica for further processing?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For further processing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And so was then the procedure about the group from Mitnica completed?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this part of the task was accomplished and the Mitnica group was taken to the collection centre at Sremska Mitrovica without any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you will agree with me that what is said here on the 19th at 1200 hours is followed by the sentence that you had been relieved from any further responsibility regarding these POWs?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You testified to Mr. Vasic that according to your recollection on that night, there were no problems. Do you remember whether Mr. Vezmarovic was present while security was provided?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was there. But whether he was there all the time, I can't say. But certainly he was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the presence of Mr. Vukosavljevic during that night, the head of security?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Dragoljub Vukosavljevic came there. He wasn't there all the time, I think, but he did come to Ovcara sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether, during that night, some local people came there to enquire who was in there, and what will happen to them?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm referring to page 8412 of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that during that night there was no intervention, no enquiries by local population or members of the TO on any grounds at the established POW camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We heard testimony here that they went there and enquired what was going to happen to those people. Not that they had any requests. Is it possible that anything like that happened?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I can say for certain, where I was, with security, which means inside the hangar, nobody was admitted. Nobody came there. Nobody enquired. I cannot say what went on outside that facility, because there was also external security outside that facility. For that part, outside the camp itself, I cannot say anything about that. But I can make statements about the situation inside the camp, because that's where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While you were inside, did you receive an information about the arrival of some drunken officer during the night? Did anybody inform you about that?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frankly, I really cannot say. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good. All right. At the moment, when you were appointed camp commander, you will agree that as of that moment the security of the camp was your responsibility?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. If you're commander, then you're responsible for the duties entrusted to you. The POWs are entrusted to you, to look after them and keep them safe under the orders of the superior command and under the orders of the superior command you will pass them on. I don't think this is unclear or problematic in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I agree. Don't mind my asking such questions, which are important to me because of some facts. So if you are camp commander, according to the principles of unity and subordination, unity of command and subordination, then you received orders and passed orders to your subordinates.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. The security or responsibility exclusively is to the camp commander for the carrying out of their tasks. That's what it's like.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who Vezmarovic was and what his responsibility was, his tasks?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vezmarovic's soldiers and the ones from the company of the military police had the task of securing those prisoners. So his role was very important and responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And he received orders directly from you?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you first, did you spend all that night inside the hanger or did you go outside also?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have gone outside a few times, but most of the time I spent inside. You'll understand, there are physiological needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you receive information or did you see, during that night, that a large group of civilians was brought to Ovcara and that a number of vehicles was left there, civilian vehicles? Do you remember anything about that?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember details. I think that there were some busses, perhaps a truck too. Those people were civilian population that was to be evacuated to the Croatian side. But the Croats refused to admit them and I think they were returned to spend the night there, and then it would be decided what would happen later. As far as I remember, that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you receive information that on the 19th or during the night of the 19th there was a number -- great number of civilians who spent the night at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it was, what it was like.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But you didn't receive any orders regarding the providing of security for those civilians?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I, as camp commander, had no authority for providing security for civilians. I have had no relevant tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Danilovic, do you know what kind of means of communications were in place between the command at Ovcara, which we call the yellow house, or the whole area of Ovcara and Negoslavci, were there any kind of communication?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that there was no wire communication. We only sent carriers, because the camp had to be established very soon and events happened very rapidly. There may have been radio communication, but I don't remember details, but we did send carriers. Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could we go into private session for a moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm now referring to the events after the 20th, when you returned. Did you learn anything about the drafting of a list of persons brought to Ovcara, and that that list was with Vojnovic?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I really didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does the name Gavrilovic mean anything to you, with regard to the facts I am asking about? Not generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I really cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I only have a few more questions and I'll be done before the pause. I'm looking at the entry dated the 18th of November where the -- where it is announced that the Mitnica group would be brought there, which actually happened. And on the following day they were taken away. You said that they had surrendered, that the surrender was preceded by negotiations about the surrender to the JNA.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I, as camp commander, had the task of organising shifts and soldiers for the -- for securing the POW camp. It was -- I was told that they were soldiers from Mitnica. About the other details, the manner of their surrender, and their changing clothes, et cetera, I'm not familiar with. I really don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Could you please take a look at the entry in the war log dated November 19th, 1800 hours. We read that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a minute. I have to find it first.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's the war log.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The war log?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The entry dated 19th of November, 1800 hours.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 19th, 1800 hours. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It was established that they were taken away and the following sentence: "That combat operations were conducted in the area of the hospital, and that the surrender of the remaining forces of ZNG and MUP is expected, and that providing security for the POW must be prepared".

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you receive any information that anybody had surrendered in the area around the hospital on the 19th or the 20th of November or were you informed about that? I'm talking about the surrender.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember whether I had any information about surrender -- surrenders at the hospital area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you receive any information about surrender of other groups of soldiers, organised surrender after the Mitnica group?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until -- or before I left to the other motorised battalion, there was nothing of the kind. After returning from the inspection of the Second Motorised Battalion, there was no official meeting about the surrender of members of the ZNG and the MUP of the Republic of Croatia in the area of the hospital about the surrender or providing security for them. So there was no discussion about that at any official meeting. I am positive about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was all I wanted to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm done with examining the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. We will have our first break and resume at ten minutes to eleven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore now has some questions for you. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Danilovic, I have some questions. You'll be pleased to hear not too many. I would like clarification about some of the things that you have said. Now when I ask these questions it is not to catch you out. I just want it to be clarified. You understand that? Is the answer yes?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. In your evidence you said that the security organs, the chief of security was authorised to issue certain orders directly to the military police. No doubt about that. What did you mean by that? I didn't quite understand.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Prosecutor, without entails, there is only certain orders, in terms of using military police as a specialised unit for certain purposes, because a security organ is the officer in a unit command providing specialised guidance, technical guidance, and he is the one best placed to advise a commander on how to use that unit. There are certain orders, such as setting up reception, and other such assignments involving command security, such orders can be issued by the chief of security. So that the unit commander is not responsible for every single order that is issued. It is for ease of handling in order to make the unit itself easier use. What that means is that the chief can issue certain kinds of orders to a subordinate unit as far as special purposes or special use are concerned, be it a MP battalion, MP platoon or MP company. So that is precisely what I had in mind when I gave that answer, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you say -- thank you very much. When you say "setting up reception," what do you mean by that? Give us an example, please.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every command has an entrance or a gate. Some sort of reception, that is normally organised. This is normally manned by soldiers or policemen. You must have enough of those. Especially if that unit has a military police unit. So this is used to filter visitors to the command in a way, in terms of identifying any persons coming in, in terms of announcing their arrival to the commander, whoever is in charge, and have the reasons clearly stated. It is for security reasons that such receptions are set up at the entrance to any headquarters or command. And this is normally the job of a security chief. That is a simple example.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, can I try and ask a simple question. Why is it -- why would a security organ be responsible for that? What attributes do they bring, to ensure that they control that situation? I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The combat rules or the rules governing the work of a security organ envisage a very specific set of criteria. I'm not sure when the last time was that I looked at those, but based on my work, as Chief of Staff, I know that it was a chief of security that I'd always task with setting up the reception area. It is not really a complicated or a difficult task, but it is certainly necessary to ensure a proper functioning, in terms of security, of any headquarters or command post. In my evidence, I pointed out that because no security was provided for the command building between the 15th and the 18th of November, 1991, an entire command was wiped out, massacred. So I'm not sure how to put this. It's not really that simple a task either. But it is not quite so difficult as to make it impossible for a security organ to carry out. However, this sort of assignment is normally left to the security organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I just read something to you. It's evidence that has been given by a witness and I would like you to, if you're able to assist us, and do so. The following question. The military police, who gave them orders? Answer: Usually it was the chief of security who issued orders to the military police, as did the Chief of Staff. Perhaps some of the operative organs, if the people I mentioned previously were absent. Question: What about the security organs, did they or were they able to give orders to the military police? Answer: Yes. Especially in professional matters. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I certainly do. I don't think there's anything contradictory about this. It certainly can happen that one of the officers in charge is away from the command at any given point in time, and that's why an operations organ chief, at the brigade command, for example, can give an assignment to the commander of a military police company. I don't think there's anything contentious about that at all, or unclear for that matter. I think that is the way it works. I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I ask you about the Mitnica evacuation. Would you mind?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at all. Why would I? I've told you all I know already and I did take a solemn oath yesterday, didn't I? The threat was 100,000 Euros or seven years of prison for perjuring myself, therefore I can hardly avoid saying what I know was the case and only the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm very grateful for the figures. I wasn't aware of them. I suspect someone else has told you and I'm not go going to be suggesting that at this point anyway, but can I just deal with Mitnica, if I may. If one sits back, looks at Mitnica and the evacuation, the control of the prisoners and the subsequent removal to Sremska Mitrovica, would it be right to say it was an operation well done and without any significant trouble?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Prosecutor, this was a long time ago and if I consider that and all of the events that followed after the evacuation, not just because I happened to be the camp commander, I'm sure the other officers would have done the same thing, but I think it is quite evident that this went smoothly. No major problems, at least. And fortunately, the first group arrived where it was supposed to arrive. I must say I deeply regret that this tragedy occurred. I regret the fact that those people were killed in such a barbaric and inhumane way. I'm not sure what sort of prison sentences were passed in relation to those 16 TO members who actually massacred those people. But I'm equally sad about these people who stand indicted in terms of command responsibility for something that happened after Mitnica. I'm sorry for providing such a broad answer to your question, but it is with the best of intentions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I ask two small favours of you. Firstly, would you avoid calling me Mr. Prosecutor. You can call me Mr. Moore, or, sir, I don't mind. I don't really like the term Mr. Prosecutor. I'm just trying to present evidence. That's the first thing. The second thing, could you just keep your answers a little shorter? In relation to the reply that you gave, what exactly do you mean "I'm equally sad about these people who stand indicted in terms of command responsibility for something that happened after Mitnica." What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My desire is to be entirely honest about this. My main reason for being so saddened is the fact that the command of the Guards Brigade or rather those members who were involved in capturing the ZNG and MUP members, if they'd wanted to have those people killed, they would have killed them during combat operations. This, however, was most certainly not the case. The Guards Brigade had as many as 30 per cent of its own officers killed, while combat operations were still underway. But it never for a moment occurred to anyone, during the actual fighting, and the capturing of these people, to even lift a finger or to do anything to these people or to harm them in any way. So if anybody could please interpret that for me, I'm sorry I just had to get it off my chest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, you see there is a problem in relation to that reply, because we've got a document and we'll show it to you in a moment from Zivota Panic on the 18th of November, where he specifically warned against the possibility of atrocities and he clearly foresaw the difficulties that not only might occur but had occurred elsewhere. Have you seen this document? Have you been shown it? It's Exhibit, I think, 415. Have you been shown that by Mr. Vasic or anybody else?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think it would only be fair for my learned friend, Mr. Moore, to give the exact reference to the witness about the document. This way we don't have the document number. We don't have the dates and perhaps it could be displayed on the screen and then the witness can answer. I think that would be the right course of action to take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The question so far, Mr. Vasic, is simply: Have you been shown it or seen it? If we go beyond that, your comment is entirely wise and appropriate. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, the first question is: Have you seen the document? Have you ever been shown the document dated the 18th of November, from the Zivota Panic to the various units?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would really like to be reminded of that particular document. It's very difficult to be specific, Mr. Moore, about this and I'm being very honest. If it's available, I would love to see it, please. Perhaps then I could give you a more specific answer. It has been a very long time, and I would definitely be hard put to remember every single detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, as I say, I think it is Exhibit 415. Can that be pulled up on the screen so everybody can see it. Have you got it in front of you?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, could you feel free --

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't say. I can't confirm that, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, can I try and help you. If one -- and feel free to read the whole document so that you don't think I'm trying to catch you out. But the core of the question really or the substance of the question can be found in paragraph 8. So would you like to take some time and read that?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine. Well, there is nothing special about this, except it is pointed out that any acts of revenge will be prevented against those captured. We all knew about this, the subordinate commands, but its all about the international law of war and the Geneva Conventions. It is all enshrined right there. I don't think there is anything very particular about this. The command of the 1st Military District focuses on this, and underlines the need for care to be taken of this at all levels of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well shall we have a look little at the paragraph 8? Shall we do that? And ask you one or two questions about it. So if we can focus on paragraph 8. Have you got it there? You can read it.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure I can. Sure I can, Mr. Moore. It's no problem the at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: "So every unit must fully control the situation on the territory of its area of responsibility". Well, that's actually a matter for any commanding officer. You agree? It's obvious.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And then a reinforcement of it. "Commanders at all levels will be responsible for this". So it's indicating it's obvious, but beware, chaps, because if you don't do it, you're going to be responsible. Yes?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Because the doctrine basically is: There is culpability when it comes to zones of responsibility. A person can be held responsible for something that may be happening within his zone of responsibility or units under his control. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Wartime laws have not entered into force and therefore, as always, nobody has the right to retribution or other kinds of revenge. Again, here we have a situation in Vukovar, it has been a extremely hard fought battle. TO units, paramilitary units and tempers are up and threats are around. So be careful. That's what it says. Do you agree? Again, nothing exceptional.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do agree with that, Mr. Moore, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. But look at the next phrase. "Which some local TOs/Territorial Defence units carried out". Now, that phrase isn't saying: May carry it out. It actually says "have already carried it out". It's in the past tense. It's not saying beware because I am looking into a crystal ball. It is saying, "beware" because some other local TOs and Territorial Defence units have carried this out. That's right, isn't it? That's the guts of paragraph 8.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, that's what it says. However, I think I can state with full responsibility that I'm not familiar with any act of retribution that was committed. I as the Chief of Staff of the 80th Motorised Brigade, there can be no doubt that these things did, indeed, occur as reflected in the order of the commander of the 1st Military District. All I'm saying is, I was not aware of anything like that. I wasn't aware of any specific areas. I wasn't aware of any specific places, or any specific TO units that committed such acts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, forgive me. There is two questions that arise out of this. You are not aware. This is coming in from Zivota Panic to Mr. Mrksic and, basically, with this sort of order, and I seem to remember it says: "Very urgent". Are you saying, therefore, as a Chief of Staff, you were not informed of the contents of this particular order?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, I believe we received an order from OG South, because this order went straight to the command of OG South. General Mrksic received this order. It was based on this order and that was the usual practice, the order was passed down on to the lower level commands. Therefore, I probably did not have this document physically available to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The reality is, you have actually no recollection of receiving any written order from Mrksic on this document. That's correct, isn't it? That's the truth? Do you remember the seven years, 100,000 Euros?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did receive the order. We did receive the warning, Mr. Moore. I never denied that, did I? I'm just saying I do not believe actually having this specific order in my hands to look at, but an order stemming from this very order was received at the command. That much is certain. It was pursuant to that order that the brigade command was supposed to take appropriate measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, can you tell us where this order is? Because nobody can find any written order at all. And you can check the war diaries, you check the operational diaries. There is nothing in there suggesting that this has been transmitted. Can you assist us with this, please?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The order simply had to arrive at the brigade command, Mr. Moore. Given the fact that it was described as very urgent and strictly confidential, this certainly would have meant that serious issues were at stake. If the order was somehow misplaced at the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade, then it should have been found at the command of OG South, because of at the very end of the order it is stated explicitly who the order is submitted to, and who it was forwarded to. You always have a list of addressees at the end of every order, who the order is supposed to be forwarded to, and you have a list of specific units that are supposed to receive an order. If there's none to be found at the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade, then it should be at the command of OG South, as having been forwarded to the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You keep using phrases "it had to", "it should have". Can we actually deal with what you know? Shall we? Shall we try and deal with the reality rather than the speculation. Now, you have no recollection, have you, of receiving a document which transmits this. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm certain that I never laid hands on this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not actually have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And if you had received this as Chief of Staff, would it be right to say that you would have issued an order yourself to subordinate commanders, knowing it was from Zivota Panic and very urgent?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, I most certainly would have written an order and I would have had it forwarded to all subordinate units. The battalion division commands and the commands of all the staff units, pursuant to an order from the command of the 1st Military District, measures are to be taken as follows in these nine items. There is nothing contentious about that. I think I would have done it, and any other officer of a similar level in the brigade command would have done the same thing, I'm positive about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What is the function of an operations diary?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, both an operations log and a war log are wartime documents. War documents. These are kept at the command and can be used to draw conclusions regarding the course of combat operations, the readiness of certain units, its losses and casualties and so on and so forth, as well as the most important moments occurring during combat operations. Wounding. Killing. Loss of lines. All taking up new positions during an attack. That is also recorded. This is a paramount document for history. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, can I suggest perhaps history only --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I suggest that perhaps history plays a slightly insignificant part at that particular time, but the function of an operations log is exactly that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It is to ensure that important orders received, orders given, or events are recorded. Would that be a fair analysis?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Moore. That's accurate. There is nothing contentious about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And would you be kind enough now, please, to just refer to the operations diary and refer to the entry showing that this Zivota Panic order was transmitted in some form to lesser commanders in your cell. Would you be kind enough to do that for us. Or might you have some difficulty doing that?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'll have to take a look, because I can't say off the top of my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, we know it arrived on the 18th. So we look after that, shall we?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I've gone to the 18th. I haven't found anything. Have you found anything?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 18th, there is -- it isn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Shall we move to the 19th?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's take a look, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I help you to say that I haven't found it. Can you find anything?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I can't see anything. It isn't entered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Shall we have a look on the 20th?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, we can have a look at the 20th, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I can't find anything on the 20th. Can you?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've scanned it as far as 1600 hours. Just a moment, please. No. It isn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You said earlier on -- and because of this rolling LiveNote I can never find what you say -- but from memory, you were not aware of incidents previously demonstrating that TOs or irregulars had behaved in a way that would place you on notice. Do you remember saying that? So what you're saying is "I didn't know about any incidents." That's what you said, I think, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be frank, I am not aware of any such incident. What the commander of the first motorised district is warning about, that there have been atrocities committed by some unit of the TO until the 18th of November, I am not familiar with that, and I really cannot speak lightly about this, but I'm sure that there has been arrogant behaviour by TO members, that is certain. Then there have been great problems with that. I remember some small details that even in the coordination of activities with TO Vukovar, without our knowledge they received financial assistance and other assistance and they used it the way they wanted without informing the commander of the town, and there have been such instances and nobody can deny that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An intervention with regard to this transcript. Page 45, line 2. This is about the staff of TO Vukovar. So the witness was speaking about the staff of TO Vukovar, that even though there was cooperation with the staff, they couldn't, et cetera. That's what they meant.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, don't worry about that. We're not talking about money here, are we? We're not talking about arrogance. Are we? We're talking about rights to retribution and other kinds of revenge. You wouldn't call that arrogance, would you?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when this qualifies as a crime, this is a very serious thing. This goes beyond arrogance. Everybody knows that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When we're talking about right to retribution and other kinds of revenge, we're talking about certainly serious physical harm and perhaps killings. That's what we're talking about, or beatings. War crimes.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, sure. We understand each other, Mr. Moore. There is nothing contentious about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, can I suggest to you if Colonel Mrksic had said to you, in a briefing: Listen in commanders, there have been beatings, atrocities, killings occurring by TO members, you would remember that, wouldn't you? Because it would place you on notice of the dangers of the same thing happening in Vukovar. That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, I, as Chief of Staff, I believe I was once or twice at the command of OG South, but that was not in an official capacity, nor did I see Colonel Mrksic, as far as I remember. Lieutenant Colonel Vojnovic, in accordance with the line of command, did go to see him, did refer about the situation in the brigade, and went to receive tasks. Such a high ranking officer must have been warned about these things, as the command of the first military district is warning about. But I did not receive knowledge about that. You should ask Lieutenant Colonel Vojnovic about these things, because he would be able to give you a good answer. I suppose that his answer would be frank and objective, as every officer should be, because the lives of their subordinates are entrusted to them. They are charged with leading their men through combat so that as few as possible are killed. And this applies also to this other aspect as the respect of the Geneva Convention and international rules of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But that's not my point. My point is perfectly simple. You are Chief of Staff. If you had been told, let us say, in documentary form, by way of an order coming from OG South, that atrocities had already occurred, committed by TO units, it is something you would remember. That is correct, is it not, because of its significance.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would have to remember. I surely would have to remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Shall we move to another topic? Let us deal with Mitnica and the security organ. You have said that Mitnica -- and I think it is generally accepted the Mitnica evacuation was almost a textbook evacuation. It was well organised, it was well performed, and there were no losses or significant troubles; that's correct, if we look at it in the round?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely accurate, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You told us in evidence and I will try and find it. Oh, yes, here we are. That an order had come to make a list. Why is it necessary to make a list in an evacuation?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Moore, that's the -- a duty and requirement so that it is known which prisoners of war, by name, were surrendered for keeping so that this is forwarded to the centre in question. A collection centre. So that people know who is supposed to be handed over and, therefore, a list is necessary. I believe that is generally known.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I suggest it's a question of common sense as well, the number of people that you have coming in should be the same number of people going out. It is just a question of common sense, and making sure that security is applied. Yes?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, Mr. Moore. We agree on that. I don't think there's anything unusual about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
