utterances.text: If we look at the Mitnica evacuation, you told us that a security officer came. My learned friend Mr. Vasic suggested, and indeed I suggest, that the security officer was a fellow called Karanfilov.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I think it was him. But don't nail me down on this. Because when I'm sure, I'm sure. I think the guy was Karanfilov but I can't tell 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What is the function of a security organ in those circumstances? Can you explain this to me?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, the security organ, in such a situation, is tasked -- at least that was customary always -- to inspect this, the carrying out of this task, which is very responsible. So he had to surrender those who were entrusted to him to someone else so they would be transferred to a collection centre and the further -- for further procedure to be conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But again just to try and help me, because in our army we don't have a security organ -- at least not that I'm aware of -- when you're talking about the security organ or the evacuation, we know the Mitnica evacuations ended in Sremska Mitrovica. Why did it go to Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Moore, it wasn't my decision as the camp commander. It was my task to accept these people, to provide accommodation for them at this camp, the POW camp - whatever we choose to call it. It doesn't matter - where they should stay for, for some time until they are transferred. Why they were transferred to Sremska Mitrovica, I can only guess. Probably the conditions for accommodation and security conditions there were such that they could stay until a decision is taken what will follow. Perhaps until it is established whether they had committed crimes in Vukovar. I can only suppose why they were sent to Sremska Mitrovica. I maybe wrong, though. Obviously in Ovcara the conditions were not satisfactory for a camp to function. There were no facilities. There was no proper accommodation. The conditions were harsh. I described them yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I suggest you're absolutely right, that Sremska Mitrovica is the obvious choice for the transfer of potential prisoners of war, or perhaps from a Serbian perspective, to clarify if there is anybody there who may have committed war crimes? It's the place that is well -- or, is able to provide accommodation and an ability to filter out suspected war criminals. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's absolutely what it was like, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And why do you say a holding facility in the Vukovar area would not be appropriate for that?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we have seen the order issued by Mr. Panic, one of the reasons was to avoid pressure being exerted from commanders of local TO units who knew the ZNG and MUP members well, so they knew perfectly well what they had been doing in the preceding month -- months, during the first and initial confrontations, because of which the JNA had to go there to protect not only the Serbian population, but all other population too. For all the well known reasons, we don't need to go into history as far as the Second World War and so on. So Vukovar certainly was not appropriate for POWs to be held for any longer stretch of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And it's much more than that. Vukovar was not appropriate for POWs to be sorted. It was a -- what I will call a facilitating or a transferring location, that is right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was a facility that was in provisional use until they are evacuated for further processing, and in accordance with the Geneva Convention and the rules and customs of war. I don't believe that is a contentious issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But why was Ovcara chosen as a detention facility, as opposed to the JNA barracks?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade, as well as the command of OG South, were at the village of Negoslavci, which means that on the 18th, when the town of Vukovar fell, there weren't even the most basic conditions, security conditions or others prevailed at the barracks of Vukovar. You and this Court are familiar that we -- with the fact that on the 22nd or 23rd requested for the barracks to be repaired, to be put into use because not even minimum conditions prevailed there. Ovcara was suitable for passing at least one night there, so that on the following day, in day light, the captured members of ZNG and MUP of Croatia can -- could be transferred. So the barracks, from our point of view, was completely unsatisfactory to accept POWs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I deal with Ovcara, the location of Ovcara and the choice of it as a detention unit. Now, this is not an exact science, it depends on the perception of the person who chooses, but with regard to Ovcara, it's right to say that it was a road that went -- one road that went through it. Secondly, it was not in a built up area, which meant that it minimised the danger of involvement from other persons. Would that be right? It was isolated.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Moore, taking into account the whole of the problems with relation to Ovcara, as of the 18th of November, it was appropriate for setting up a camp for the collection of POWs in a safe manner, until conditions for their accommodation at the main collection centre in Mitrovica are created. And they could also be transmitted or emitted -- evacuated in a safe manner. I'm talking about the first group. And that's how -- what should have happened to the second group, also. What you are saying is not contentious. It is an isolated facility. There is a road leading to it, and out of it. So that under wartime conditions a brief stay of captured army members was possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Why do you say in your evidence, That's what happened with the first group and that's what should have happened to the second group? Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying that because Ovcara -- in Ovcara, there were minimum conditions for the evacuation of prisoners of war without any problems. So if it was possible to do that with the first group, then it should have been possible to do that in the same manner with the second group, that should have been taken to Sremska Mitrovica. I have no special -- other information about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now can you try to throw your mind back to Mitnica when you were there, the night of the 18th. I want to deal with that time specifically. When you go to Mitnica. You remain at Mitnica. So I want to deal with that, please. Was there at any time -- sorry, there's an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was at Mitnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether possibly the interpretation is wrong, but it is suggested that my witness was at Mitnica, which is not the case. We never heard that he was at Mitnica. He was only commanding the group that came from Mitnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Sorry, I put the question because we talked about the Mitnica evacuation. I want to talk about the Mitnica evacuation. My fault. I think you understood that anyway.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I just want to deal with the Mitnica evacuation and obviously it is at Ovcara. So I want you to think about that, if you'd be kind enough. You say that things went well. Is there anything that you can remember that caused what I would call a smell of fear that might have caused people to be terrified and literally I use the phrase "a smell of fear"? Anything that happened when you were there to cause that?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Moore, I can say quite honestly and with full responsibility that I had no fear at all with regard to the prisoners taken in the area of Mitnica. I don't know who could have been in fear. Maybe the prisoners themselves, but I really did threaten the commander of that group. I don't remember his name. And I said to him: Listen here, don't you try to run or -- or do anything else that's funny, because fire will be opened. So don't do that because it would be a very dumb thing to do. And I guarantee that you will safely transfer to the collection centre where it will be determined what will happen to you afterward. So of course I cannot now go into conjectures, whether anybody was in fear or not. That's my personal opinion anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, I would suggest all you did was, you told the leader of the Mitnica group: "Behave. And if you behave, nothing will happen to you." In summary, that's what you said, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't exactly reproduce my conversation with him, but that's basically what it was. And if he was here as a witness, he would have been able to confirm that. And all that I have said so far, yesterday and today, confirms that. So you, of course, can say when you don't agree with something. But I do remember some detail from that period and I think that's -- that it all was that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: From memory, there were 181 people, I think. 181 or 182. Prisoners inside the hangar. The people guarding them, would it be right to say they operated in shifts? Can we just keep your answers short on this, please.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were security shifts. I think there were two such shifts. There were no problems with those shifts. As far as I remember, there were 181 or 182 possibly, but I know that that was the figure. There were that many people inside the hangar. The shifts took turns, one or two-hour shifts, I can't remember, but it was very cold obviously and you couldn't keep people just standing there in the cold with their rifles at the ready. And the shifts may have been one-hour shifts or two-hour shifts, but they were rotating, regularly, and they were guarding those prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And with regard to the hangar itself, it was what I will use the phrase "pretty packed", fairly full of individuals inside. There was 181, plus the security detail. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And for lighting, did you use -- I think you used vehicle lights originally; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't quite remember that of all things, and I would not like to be speculating about this, so say anything that was in fact wasn't the case. I don't think that was the main problem we had. Our main trouble was the cold and we tried to deal with that by using the haystacks in that part of the hangar where the security were deployed. We gave them those to use so they had something to lie down on top of, and warm up a little. As for the call of nature, we tried to use those buckets and cans. We tried to improvise in the corners of the hangar. It wasn't possible to have each individual leave the hangar to respond to the call of nature. That wasn't possible to organise. So this is what we did. And I don't think it was a problem really.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask about the toileting facilities, but what I am going to suggest to you is that if you want to deal with security with 181 people, it is essential to have light and an ability to see what they might be doing. Would you agree with that? You're not just going to have 181 people sitting in the dark, are you?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, there was some lighting. I can't say that it came from a motor vehicle. There were lamps, batteries, torches, but there was lighting and all movement among the prisoners could clearly be discerned. The distance between those captured and their guards was no more than three or four metres, I would say up to four metres at most.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, are you saying, then, that somebody who would come to a door of the hangar, because it was packed and there was lighting, they would be able to see people inside?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be difficult. There were guards at the entrance and no one was allowed inside without approval by the commander, approval by the camp commander, and that was me. No one was allowed inside without my approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What about if someone came and came in and saw only a group of 50 or 60 people, in a group looking absolutely terrified. Does that correspond with your memory of the 18th of November, and the Mitnica evacuation? No one else seen, just 50 or 60, with complete fear in their faces. Did that occur in the Mitnica evacuation?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that they were afraid for the fate they would eventually meet, but I didn't consider that a problem at the time. I did warn their man in charge that nothing whatsoever would befall them, that they wouldn't come to any grief, but at the other end of the hangar you have all of those guards -- I did provide guarantees to these people that they would come to no harm at all, and that was as much as I could do under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It's clearly the way I'm putting the question. But I will ask it again. Let us assume that a person goes into the hangar, actually into the hangar. Do you think it's feasible that he would only be able to see 50 people, just in a group, and not be able to see the remaining 150?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this is precisely what Mr. Moore was objecting about earlier. He is asking the witness to speculate. Would a person coming in see this many or that many people? How could the witness possibly know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Your answer, Mr. Vasic, may turn on the lighting and how the prisoners were grouped inside, so the witness may be able to comment. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I suggest the following to you. That if a person went to the door of the hangar or went slightly inside the hangar, they would not just be aware of 50 people. They would be perfectly aware there would be a large number, almost 150 others in that relatively small hangar. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Moore, they were how should I put it? Cramped, packed tightly together in that far half of the hangar and they were better off that way. They were a lot warmer. It was easier for them to survive the night like that. Many knew each other so they talked and talked and several times I had to warn them about talking loud. I had to ask them to lower their voices and whisper, because we the guards were greatly bothered by this, as the whole thing went on. As for how many people a person could spot on the way in, well, that really depends. It was a rather small area. That's a fact. But in this specific situation, under those specific circumstances, if you have 15, 16 or 17 guards, for example, watching over 180 men, I as an officer saw no other way to do this. And this is eventually what we did. Was I wrong? Was I right? That's a matter that needs evaluating.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I'm not going to express any view right or wrong. That's not my task. But can I just move on to one or two other little areas. Nothing actually happened at Mitnica to cause any difficulty or concern, that is right, isn't it? There wasn't any crisis, any significant problem, was there?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No problem. But in the circumstances under which those 180 people had been taken or the specific area -- well, this is something that I'm not familiar with, and I don't wish to be speculating. They were concerned for their lives, you could tell that in their faces. And that is beyond dispute. Nobody can deny that. The situation was what it was. It was my task to make sure they were safe. Once they were evacuated we would leave it to others to take care of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm not trying to fetter your reply in any way, please understand that. But could you try and keep your answers a little shorter? If you feel you have to say it, do say it. But can you just try and consciously keep them shorter. So it's right to say, there was nothing immediate that caused concern; there was no event that caused concern? That is right, isn't it? Nothing out of the ordinary?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think not, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. That's capable of two interpretations, when you say "I think not," do you mean that there wasn't any problem?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, security-wise, we had no problem. Its an individual matter. It really depends on which each of the prisoners were feeling at the time, under what circumstances they had been taken, what they had been doing up to the time of their arrest, their individual responsibilities. It's very difficult for me to go into that. This was the very first time in my life I put eyes on most of those people anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Were you in radio control or contact? Were you in radio contact with any other units?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which specific unit you have in mind, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, any units. Did you have a radio capability at that time?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, there was a connection to the brigade command. I don't think we had a line open to any of the subordinate units. There was no communication capability between the compound and subordinate units. I don't think so, but that wasn't necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you, at any time, contact the brigade command to say: We need help, or we have a problem? We need help?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. There weren't no problems to begin with. Why would I want to create one, since there were none? So, no, I requested no assistance simply because everything was going according to plan. And there was no need for me to request assistance. I don't know where you got this from. Maybe it's something someone stated, but what I'm telling you is what I, as the camp commander, know with sure and set knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So whoever would state that would state it in error? That's correct, isn't it? That's what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I wish to say is, that is erroneous. Absolutely. There was no trouble. I could start making things up, but it's pointless and it's speculation. If you say that assistance was requested on the night of the 18th, during the night and by 1830 hours the next day when this group was taken to Sremska Mitrovica, I think that would be responsible for me to issue any statements or assessments like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I just please once again say: Keep your answers shorter. I am not, in any way, suggesting that you have behaved improperly. Do you understand that? Please understand that. I am not suggesting you behaved improperly. In actual fact I would suggest you behaved properly. Now, can we move on, please? You have told us that you remember -- you seem to remember anyway a police unit attending. Do you remember saying that in evidence? Yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was the military police company of the 80th Motorised Brigade or rather an element of that unit which was involved in guarding the POWs, that is quite accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So as far as you can recollect, that is the only unit that came that evening to Ovcara to deal with the Mitnica evacuation? Is that correct, or not?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, this unit was required to guard the captured ZNG and MUP members as part of a security regime that was in place. I can hardly be expected to say whether there were perhaps a few of the reconnaissance company men involved. Please don't expect me to provide a specific figure as to how many soldiers were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That's not what I'm asking. I am dealing with a very simple issue. As far as you're aware, once the unit that was guarding these prisoners was at Ovcara, that was the unit or the attached members who stayed with the prisoners until they left the next day.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. That's right, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I know it's a little early for the break, but I have a reason for asking if Your Honour could take the break now. It may be that the Court time will be saved in the long run, and I know that that is always an attractive proposition to Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Moore. We will resume at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Danilovic, you were being asked about OG South. When did OG South cease as a being? You thought after the 20th, somewhere around the 22nd. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 22nd or the 23rd. I think we discussed that yesterday. Don't hold me to it, but I know that that was when the Partisan Brigade -- or rather, the 80th Brigade took over the area of responsibility from the 20 Partisan Brigade, Jakobolac [phoen], Ovcara, as well as some other villages in the general area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was after that that the brigade command started to operate independently and was now outside OG South, on the 22nd or possibly the 23rd. But please don't hold me to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting you're wrong. I'm going to show you a document in a minute. What is the function -- in very short order, please -- what is the function of a regular combat report? In very brief terms, just describe it to us.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, a regular combat report must be an overview of the combat readiness of a given unit, as well as an overview of the development over the last 24 hours. Those that are most important and those that might affect the combat readiness of a unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm going to try to deal with this quickly. I want you to look, please, at Exhibit 426. So could Exhibit 426 be put on the monitor, please. Can you tell me, please, when you've had it on the monitor or when you can see it.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's right there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let's look at the top, OG -- basically OG South. And the time is 1800 hours, 23rd November. Hmm?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's right. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Negoslavci. Clearly it's to the command of the 1st Military District. Regular combat report. Important point, I'd suggest, is that the 23rd of November, 6 o'clock in the evening, as we say it as lay people, and when we turn to page 2 there it is. It is signed by Colonel Mrksic. Can we turn over the page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I must say I'm listening to the B/C/S interpretation and I think it is very difficult for the interpreters to keep abreast with my learned friend. I think half the question is there, and half is missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I will go slowly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we just start again. We've got the document on the screen. It says: "Regular combat report". The important point I would suggest, it's from OG South command. The timing is 1800 hours, 23rd of November, and when we turn to page 2, if that can be done, please, have you got page 2 yet?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And there we can see stamped for receipt 23rd of November, signed by Colonel Mrksic. So can I suggest to you that in actual fact if one works from this document, you are quite right, it is actually the 23rd of November. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let's move on to one or two other topics. Yesterday when you were giving your evidence I closed my eyes and I asked myself, what is this man saying? And it seems to be that you are suggesting that the LAD was never subordinated to OG South. That's one of the things. Now, is that what you're actually trying to say?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm truly sorry, Mr. Moore, for giving rise to this misunderstanding. The 80th LAD PVO throughout the fighting and ever since its arrival in the deployment area, meaning the general Vukovar area, remained under the direct command of the commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade. It was not at any time resubordinated in its entirety to any other unit. The fact remains that some batteries from the anti-aircraft defence units were at various times attached to other units, but for individual missions. Nothing more. I'm not sure if we understand each other better now, but that was my original meaning. So if you misunderstood my original answer, then this would be a new one and hopefully a clearer one, for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't blame yourself. Sometimes I don't quite follow the point and it is usually my fault. But can we look at one or two of the entries of the war diary. And that is -- if I can just get my reference -- it's Exhibit 375, I believe. Now, you've been asked some of these questions, but I want to try to just deal with it fairly sharply. We have got on the 10th of November -- have we got that, 1600 hours?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, if one looks at that, we've got LAD PVO is operating according to OG South plans and combat tasks. You've already been referred to that, haven't you? Have you got that?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Moore. Indeed. If I may just clarify something. The order for the anti-aircraft defence, chief of PVO, Operations Group South, what you saw there was the assignments for all PVO units and the order was served on all the units. The order to unify all operations against any aircraft flying over the area, the meaning being the LAD PVO was to act on this order that had arrived from the command of OG South and, needless to say, pursuant to the orders of the brigade commander. The LAD PVO was not separate as a unit. It would have been quite ridiculous for the commander of OG South to be in command of the 80th Motorised Brigade and again also the LAD PVO, that would constitute dual command, which is unimaginable in the army that I served in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. You have told us this but I'm going to try to quickly take you to various parts. I would like you to, then, see or have presented Exhibit 367, because that perhaps is the core of the problem, if it be a problem. And then we will come back to the war diary. Now, have you got 367 on your screen?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I haven't got it, but never mind. The front page should say the 9th of November, the 9th of the 11th, 1991. Village of Negoslavci, to the command of the 80th LAD PVO. So we can see, quite clearly, this order is directed to that particular unit. Do you agree? Can you just answer.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, could I please look at the entire order? If we can please scroll it down a little.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We will go on to the order, but I want to deal so that everybody knows where we're -- the date we're dealing with. If we look at the top of the page, we've got command of OG South. We've got the 9th or the 11th. It is important to get that into perspective and to whom it is directed, namely to the command of the 80th LAD PVO. Now, can we just move on, as long as you agree with that. And what I would like to do --

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This order is addressed to the command of the LAD PVO, as an order regulating anti-aircraft combats within OG South. This is specifically in reference to the 80th LAD PVO. If you ask me, it is not the nature of this order to suggest that the 80th LAD PVO was specifically subordinated to any other unit within OG South. When you asked me a while ago, it would have been quite illogical for the commander of OG South to be in charge of both the 80th Motorised Brigade and the 80th LAD PVO at the same time, given the fact that the 80th LAD PVO was, in fact, part of the 80th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm not trying to catch you out. I'm trying to direct your mind to a piece of evidence. Now, can we try to do that, please? So let's go to what I would call number 7, so it's number 7 itself, where it deals with the headings of ammunition and missile consumption. So can we go right forward to that. Now, have you got that part? If we look at paragraph 7, do we not have the fact that the LAD PVO of the 80th Motorised Brigade is to provide security for the real units of OG South until the 11th of November? And thence the security of the 80th Motorised Brigade? Now it's clearly in an order. So it tends to suggest, perhaps, to people looking at this, that you're talking about the LAD of the 80th, I will use the word subordinated in a neutral sense, protecting the real units of OG South and, then, realigning itself with the 80th Motorised Brigade. Do you agree with that or not? Is that what it seems to say?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, this has jogged my memory a little. The real battalion of the 80th Motorised Brigade was on the move on the 9th between Smederevo and Sotin, I believe. They were supposed to move along that axis and redeploy so that they could provide adequate support to all the units there, including the 80th LAD PVO. The reason being the brigade's rear battalion was not what it was supposed to be. And the division had to go into action and that is why that was made available for support for the benefit of Operations Group South, and that is precisely what this order indicates. I hope that resolves your dilemma. If you're now satisfied, well, fine. If not, we can try to go deeper into this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, thank you for that kind offer, but regrettably I'm not quite satisfied and I want to deal with one or two other topics. Would you mind? So we go back, then, to the exhibit dealing with the war diary. So we have the 10th of November, which corresponds with this order at 6 o'clock, 10th of November, exactly in the timespan that that order designates, and it says: "LAD PVO is operating according to the OG South plan and combat tasks". Can I suggest to you that that entry reflects the order that we have just seen. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Moore, I do not wish to create any disagreements that are not strictly necessary between us. But I explained about the LAD PVO being deployed as a support unit for OG South. I explained about that, and that's in reference to that. What it says here about them, performing tasks according to a plan produced by OG South, the reference here is to the general order that was passed along by OG South to all of their subordinate units. And believe me, I state this with full responsibility as a military officer. If you don't take my word for it, you might as well get an expert to confirm what I'm telling you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we just forget about the personal element. No one is trying to say that you're deliberately misleading or you're incorrect. I'm not trying to suggest that, so please relax in relation to that, and let's just look at this particular document. "LAD PVO is operating according to OG South plan and combat tasks". That is a direct reflection of what I've just shown you. That, I would suggest, must be correct. Don't you agree?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Moore, I do acknowledge your role in this Court, but I tried to give you a simple example for what I'm saying. It would have been anything but normal for the commander of OG South to command the 80th Motorised Brigade and, apart from that, separately, command the LAD PVO. From a military perspective, this would be beyond reason. I don't want to insult anybody, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What you were concerned about is duality of line of command. That is what you're talking about, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said why, so I've stated the reasons. And it's only because of the security support of this unit for OG South, and that's why this order was passed, to regulate support, security until the support battalion arrives at the area. We believe we can find this in the operations log, and compare the entries, if there is a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, let's move on to the 11th and then I will come to the point and move on to another topic. If we deal with the 11th of November, 1800 hours, the point's already been made. LAD PVO are still in the same positions. Do you see that entry? I think you've already been referred to it.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, all right. That's clear enough, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I ask you to go to the 15th of November. This is something you have not been asked about.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So, let's see what it says for November 15th. 1800 hours, did you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't want to deal with the LAD PVO. I want to deal with another unit. So have you got the 15th of November? 1600 hours?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 15th?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Have you got that?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Sorry, that's my fault. I think it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is in the transcript in error one point earlier as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: 1800 hours, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Yes. I don't know which unit you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I want to deal with the OKB, have you got it?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What is the OKB?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an armoured battalion, Mr. Moore, that's the abbreviation that is commonly used. This battalion was resubordinated to the 130th Motorised Brigade, so it was not attached to the 80th Motorised Brigade to which it originally belongs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I'm not trying to suggest it is. But let's just look at the language used. "The OKB is", note the word "still under the command of the 130th Motorised Brigade and operating on 103rd Motorised Brigade combat tasks". You actually used the words "resubordinated" to reflect the words "under the command", isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see where 103rd. This reads the OKB is part of the 103rd -- is attached to the 130th Motorised Brigade and operating on combat tasks of the representatives of the command. This is what it says. Well, it isn't really the proper military style.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, let's just see actually what you said. It's an armoured battalion, Mr. Moore. That's an abbreviation which is commonly used. And the following words "this battalion was resubordinated to the 130th Motorised Brigade". So you are using the word "resubordinated" in place of the phrase "under the command". Is that right, or not?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, both are correct. So when a unit is resubordinated then it is under the command of the unit to which it was resubordinated. I don't think that is a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Can we then just turn, please, to the following. Let's go to the 12th of November.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I have to go back. Let me just find it. At what hour, Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Exactly the same hour. So if we go to the 12th, we've got PVO is still at the same positions. LAD PVO was still at the same positions. And then it goes on about the second LAD, the third LAD and then the following phrase: "They continue to proceed in line with OG South combat tasks." So does that mean, therefore, that OG South combat tasks are controlling their position?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, the entire 80th Motorised Brigade is active in accordance with the plans of OG South. I believe that this is mentioned in the war log only because we received a special order for anti-aircraft defence, which includes all anti-aircraft units as far as general tasks and the control of air space are concerned. There was no other reason for the entire 80th LAD PVO to be subordinated to OG South. Why should the command of OG South have two units on their line of command? There was no need for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, you have told us that the word "resubordinated" in place of the phrase "under the command", you say both are correct. So when a unit is resubordinated, then it is under the command of the unit to which it is resubordinated. Let's look now at the 13th of November. Can we just look at the entry for the LAD PVO. Have you got it?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found it. But the one who wrote this phrased this in a funny way. I'm speaking as a professional soldier now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you just answer the question, please --

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But you know --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: -- rather than answer before the question is posed. Because if what you say is right, this particular entry "it is under OG South command" means in actual fact, by what you have said earlier on, it's resubordinated. I see you nodding in agreement with that. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Moore. I am constantly trying to tell you what it was really like. I cannot explain why the operation's officer made this entry in this -- in the log the way he did. But I can show -- if there is an order, according to which the LAD PVO was resubordinated to OG South, if we can find that, I will apologise to you, because the resubordination cannot be conducted based on some oral agreement. Only in exceptional circumstances, if the situation is extremely grave. But under any other circumstances, this can only be done based on a written document. You can verify that any time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well that raises two issues, but let's deal with the first. The first is, if a person reads this diary and these words, "it is under OG South command" it means, whether you agree with it or not, it means that the LAD PVO is resubordinated and under the command of OG South. That is correct, isn't it? That's what those words suggest. You may disagree, but that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Moore, I insist that they were not resubordinated to OG South. I gave you a simple example why would the commander of OG South single out LAD PVO as a separate unit. So to have two units to command both the 80th Motorised Brigade and the LAD PVO? I don't know how much you know about military terminology, I don't want to insult you or anybody else here, but that's how things are. That's why I said I really would like to see the order for the resubordination of LAD PVO to OG South. But look at the entry under LAD PVO. This says: The HAD 105 millimeters. It says on the orders of OG South, delivered fire on the orders of OG South. If we were to follow this line of thinking, we would also conclude that this HAD was also resubordinated of OG South, which was not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would suggest that is not the case at all. And you should not assume that you're the only person in this building with military service. Can we just deal, please, with this particular entry. Is it right that the words in this diary, that if they are taken at face value, irrespective of what you say and the Court can weigh it up themselves, if you look at the words, it actually means that the LAD PVO is resubordinated to OG South. Whether you like it, whether you don't, that's what the words mean, isn't that right? Can we have an answer, please.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, I was Chief of Staff of the brigade and I insist that the 80th LAD PVO was never resubordinated to the command of OG South, which you can verify. This is my opinion. I didn't want to slight anybody's military expertise. If that's your impression, I do apologise sincerely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I can assure you my military expertise is a lot less than yours. Let's move on to a different topic, shall we? When one looks at what you are saying in evidence here, are you actually saying that (redacted) was to blame or had responsibility for the killings at Ovcara? Is that what you're actually saying?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, I really cannot anticipate anybody's guilt, that's up to the Court to decide. Please do not lead me in the direction of stating my personal opinion. I'm only saying what things were really like at those times of war, and I would never venture to forecast any decision of the Court. I'm here to tell the truth, and nothing but the truth. I trust that we understand each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We do understand each other. Can we understand each other in the following terms, that the 80th Motorised Brigade, that was the zone of responsibility for that unit? The Ovcara hangar was within that zone of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not at all contentious, Mr. Moore. That is obvious, from all the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. We agree on that. If the commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade informs his senior officer that something is happening within the zone of responsibility of the commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade, if I read the regulations correctly, that means that the commander of OG South has the responsibility to deal with the problem. Is that right, or not?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, how do I put this? Every commander, in accordance with the decision and the tasks, carries out those tasks in his zone of responsibility. If the commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade reports to the superior command that he requests help or assistance of any kind, then the superior command is required to take adequate measures to resolve the problem that has arisen. I cannot assess how the commander of the 80th Brigade requested any of the assistance, or what he has done. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let's deal with the reality because we're going round in circles in this case. The reality is, if Vojnovic as the commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade is aware of something happening within his zone of responsibility, then informs his superior officer that there are problems within Vojnovic's zone of responsibility, Mrksic, who is the commander, has the responsibility transferred to him. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As long as he is in the zone of responsibility, that is the 80th Motorised Brigade, within the OG South, the commander is responsible for that zone. The commander of each unit is responsible for his zone of responsibility. This applies to the 80th Motorised Brigade and OG South also, and General Mrksic is responsible for everything that goes on in the zone of responsibility of his units -- his unit, and the units subordinated to his unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let us deal with lines of command. Let us take a situation where we are talking about the zone of responsibility of the 80th Motorised Brigade. Clearly the zone of responsibility is the responsibility of Vojnovic as a superior officer, do you agree?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we're speaking about the zone of responsibility of the 80th Motorised Brigade, then the most responsible person is the commander. This is general knowledge, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, is the answer "yes" to my question?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the unit commander is responsible. That's my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That's Vojnovic?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the commander of the 80th, Lieutenant Colonel Vojnovic, is responsible for his zone. I can't say anything but that. So every commander is responsible for his zone of responsibility. Another issue is, if I may take a little more of your time? Another issue is whether or not it is necessary for the superior commander, that is the commander of the OG South, to participate in the resolving of some problem. I'm now only talking about the objective responsibility for a given zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So I will try one more time. If we have a situation where the zone of responsibility -- the 80th Motorised Brigade, it would be Vojnovic. That's right, isn't it? He's the commander -- that's right? How come you're not saying "yes"? Don't you know?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the commander of the 80th Brigade is responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If a commander sees something occurring within his zone of responsibility, which he has never been informed of, and he, because he wishes to do so, goes to see his superior officer to clarify what on earth has been happening, what is the responsibility of that superior officer once he's been told that by Vojnovic?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise, but I have not really understood the question. If you could repeat it, please. I didn't understand it well enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We have the zone of responsibility of the 80th Motorised Brigade. The 80th Motorised Brigade is caught within OG South. The commander of the 80th brigade is Vojnovic. If we take the situation where Vojnovic finds something occurring within his zone of responsibility, which he is firstly unaware of by its happening, and, two, who is there, and he then goes to his commander, namely Mrksic, Mr. Mrksic, and tells him: There is something going on within my zone of responsibility, namely the 80th, which is clearly your zone of responsibility, OG South, it's right, isn't it, that Mrksic becomes involved in the process because he's been informed? That's what command responsibility is about, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now this is an issue of command responsibility. In the concrete case, Lieutenant Colonel Vojnovic should have checked all the circumstances -- I don't know, now, I'm now speaking hypothetically. If he was unaware of any events, he should have checked what had happened, and then requested assistance. I don't know what kind of assistance he had requested from General Mrksic. I'm not -- I'm not familiar with all of these things. It would be best to ask him, because I couldn't say anything of that nature, but certainly every commander is responsible for his zone of responsibility. The town commander for the town, the brigade commander for another area and the commander of OG South for the entire area covered by his subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I believe I've asked you a perfectly straightforward question. I know you're a witness for Colonel Mrksic, but you also are a witness for the Court and you say that you want to seek truth. Now I will ask this question one more time. Do you understand? And I will repeat it. If you have a situation where Vojnovic, as the commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade, finds something happening within his zone of responsibility, which causes him considerable concern, and he then goes to his superior, namely Colonel Mrksic, are you saying that Mrksic has no responsibility? Now, kindly answer that question in a simple way, please.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a complex question, Mr. Moore. The guilt must be established in terms of command. You are now asking me to say who is guilty. I cannot go into that. The events that happened must be fully investigated. The circumstances must be clear why the event happened, and after that, inferences can be made about who bears the greatest responsibility in that chain of command, although to be frank, the very notion of command responsibility is a rather flexible thing to me. It's like the brigade commander learns of -- if you just let me finish -- learns of a crime committed by some group and now we're chasing the brigade commander because he can't really hold the hands of 5.000 soldiers and tell them how to behave. Morally, of course, he is responsible, but the most concrete responsibility lies with the one who committed the concrete crime. As we cannot -- the same way we cannot say that a whole people is guilty because some persons who belonged to that people committed a crime, and it's much the same way with a military commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that my learned friend is pushing the witness to speculate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic. I do not agree. The witness's answer is speculating, but not the question that was put to him. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I will not move away from this topic unless ordered to by the Court. Do you understand? I have given you a situation. I've absolutely no doubt you know perfectly well the reason why it's being asked. You say you've come to tell the truth and I'm suggesting to you if Vojnovic tells Mrksic, as his superior commander, that incidents are happening within the zone of responsibility of OG South as well as the 80th Motorised Brigade, Mrksic is informed of the matter and he is responsible. That is right, isn't it? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Moore, I think in that case you should ask both Mr. Mrksic and Mr. Vojnovic. They'll tell you what it was about and why. I can hardly be expected to blame, either. I'm not familiar with the circumstances. I was not at the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade at the time and anything that I might say would be fortuitous, in a way. These men should be asked how this whole thing came about. You should talk to them. It is very difficult for me to be the judge of this particular matter. You have all my sincerest apologies but you should hear these people out. They'll tell you about the circumstances which brought this about. And then you will be able to draw an objective conclusion as to individual guilt. I'm not sure if that satisfies your ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to attribute guilt. That's not a matter for you. It's not a matter for me. It's a matter for the Bench. Do you understand? I suggest you are deliberately avoiding answering this question. That's what I'm suggesting. And you know perfectly well that if that scenario is correct, Mrksic has responsibility. It's as simple as that. Just on the line of command. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, I'm so sorry that we seem to be talking at cross-purposes. You are demanding a specific answer from me, and to apportion blame. I remain adamant about telling you this. You should hear out both these commanders. They will tell you about the circumstances of this event. They will tell you about the multiple causes, what brought this about. Once you've heard that, you will be better equipped to judge whose fault it was and who is to blame for what happened, with all due respect, sir. Please don't get me wrong. Please don't leave me in this position. Please don't expect me to assess these commanders. I was elsewhere when this unfortunate event occurred. I had been speaking about all of the places that I was physically present at and all of the developments that I personally was in a position to effect. In this particular instance, I was 20 kilometres away from there and there was nothing I could do about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I will let the Court draw their own inferences if they deem it appropriate. I will move on to another topic. Let us take a situation where you have a zone of responsibility, and let us say it is the 80th Motorised Brigade and you have persons come into that zone of responsibility who are from the superior command. What then is the person whose zone of responsibility it is, what is that person to do if someone comes into that zone of responsibility from the superior command? Do you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Mr. Moore. That depends on who it is coming into the zone of responsibility of a unit. They would first be required to report to the most senior officer and to explain their mission and reason for being in this particular zone of responsibility, that is the done thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It may well be the done thing, but if it isn't done, if a -- an officer or officers from the superior command come into that zone of responsibility and don't introduce themselves and say "we're here because of A, B, or C," what is that officer in charge of the zone of responsibility, what is he to do? What is his position?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This officer -- unless the arrival of these persons has been announced, cannot but send these persons away from his zone of responsibility. At least that's what I would do. As for anybody else, well, that's their own business.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But bearing in mind they're from the superior command, is not one of the options to clarify from the superior command why they're there?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do agree with you, Mr. Moore. That is also something that is done in these cases. You would put a call through to the superior command, but this is rarely, if ever, the case. This sort of thing doesn't happen that often. The questions should then be: Why have you sent this group of officers? What's their mission? And what exactly are they supposed to be monitoring? If a negative reply is received from the superior command, then these people are sent away. At least, these are the steps that ought to be taken in a situation like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So what you're saying is that one clarifies with the superior command. They clarify whether in actual fact the unit should be there, or not, and if the unit should be there as a consequence of the superior command's orders, then they have priority. That is right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't understand your question. Who has priority? If you could please run that past me again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You have the superior command. Let us say, in this case, it is OG South. OG South has got priority or is the senior to the 80th Motorised Brigade. That's correct. You know that.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Most certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let us deal, then, with the zone of responsibility of the 80th. Let us assume for a moment a unit comes into the zone of responsibility for the 80th. And that unit is from the superior command. Now, you have told us that the unit from the superior command should approach the 80th commander, or whoever is in command and say: We are here because. You've already told us that. Now all I'm saying is, if in actual fact the command -- the commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade contacts the superior command, let us say Mrksic, and Mrksic says "Well, they're from the superior command." The superior command unit has the priority in the zone of responsibility of the 80th, doesn't it? Because it comes with the orders from the superior command. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my apologies, Mr. Moore, but you seem to be using two concepts there. First, you're asking me, if a group of officers arrived in the brigade's zone of responsibility, what would the procedure be and now you're saying, if a unit arrived, and -- these two concepts are slightly at odds to say the least but the procedure applied seems to be the same. If, indeed, it arrived, although this is very exceptional, then the commander of the 80th should put a call through to the command of OG South to enquire about the reasons why the unit had been sent to him. Based on the answer received, the commander then decides whether he will absorb the unit, if indeed they are there on orders from a superior unit, or if on the other hand he gets a reply from the OG South commander saying, no, I never sent that unit to your zone of responsibility, then he will just send them packing. I'm not sure if that makes it any clearer, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, it makes it very clear and I think we're absolutely in agreement. But can I deal with this, then. It's right, isn't it -- and I think you've already told us -- that in actual fact there was never any indication of any evacuation from the hospital coming through Ovcara. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know -- well, actually, I don't quite understand. What do you mean the evacuees from the hospital passing through or coming through Ovcara? I'm not really sure. Can you please repeat that question for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, I'll repeat the following. You had no indication, you were not informed that there was anybody coming through from the hospital which the -- which your unit, the 80th Motorised Brigade had responsibility for. You never received any indication that that was going to happen, did you?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's either in the operations log or in the war log, I can't quite remember, but you have an indication there that preparations were ordered to receive prisoners from the hospital. It was written down there that shifts were to be set up in order to set up a security regime for that purpose. We can go through the two logs, if you like, but it's right there. I saw it recorded there, which means that the arrival of this group of prisoners from the hospital was expected.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I suggest while there is an entry in the log, that in actual fact it is not a specific order. It is merely a warning order that there is a possibility that that might occur.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, it's either in the operations log or in the war log, but it's certainly there. It says that the brigade commander orders -- feel free to use that word, because it definitely applies -- that steps be taken to ensure the prisoners from the hospital are received and that a security system is set up for guarding them. That's what it says. I'm not sure what else it could possibly mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Then can you explain how it is you mentioned to this Court, gave evidence to this Court in the following way in answer to my learned friend Mr. Vasic, the following question: Did you receive any information that anybody had surrendered in the area around the hospital on the 19th or the 20th of November, or were you informed about that? I'm talking about the surrender. And this is the answer you gave. I do not remember whether I had any information about surrender, surrenders at the hospital area. Now, can you explain to me how it is you gave that reply at 31, 6 today. When I give the reference, it's the time. How you're able to give that answer and yet, now, you say there was an order given. Can you explain the inconsistency?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Moore, I don't think there is any inconsistency there. That's what it says. It's either in the operations log or in the war log. You have the brigade commander there ordering shifts to be set up, and for the prisoners taken in the hospital area in Vukovar to be put up. Since I wasn't there at the time, when these prisoners were brought in, I can't tell you much about the specific circumstances of the case in hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So are you saying, therefore, that you actually don't know, but you're working from the log?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. Yes, that's precisely the case. I'm working from the log.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So you have no personal knowledge? You are using the log.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't physically present at the command at the time. I'm not sure if you understand that. I was elsewhere on a different mission at the time. And I'm not sure how to put this. I wasn't up to date on anything, every little thing that was going on. But I have the log for that, the log says that a surrender of POWs is expected in the hospital area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Were you ever told -- well, you wouldn't have because you have no personal knowledge of it. Let's move on to another topic. Is your father called Vlado, V-l-a-d-o?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. The late Vlado.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And the village, I will attempt to spell it rather than pronounce it. Z-l-i-j-e-b, does your family come from that location?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name of the village is Zdrijelo. That's where I was born. I'm not sure how that is relevant to our discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Were you ever a commander of the 3rd Mountain Infantry Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The mountain brigade? Never. I was commander of the 3rd Podrinje light infantry brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So where were you in March, 1993?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, I would like to kindly ask you to not ask me to share information with you about my involvement in the war in the Republika Srpska. I have not been granted a waiver in relation to that sort of information. If you could please continue to ask me questions about anything that you might deem to be relevant to this trial, because that is what I am here for. To be quite honest, specifically, I really can't see any possible link between this trial, this case, and my involvement at the front line in the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. I object to this sort of question. This is outside the framework of the indictment. We've had a situation like that in this case with Mr. Imra Agotic when my colleague, Mr. Lukic was asking him questions about 1993. And the ruling of the Trial Chamber to the effect that that had no relevance at all. And was not in any way linked to our own case. We have the specific reference, 2124 and 2125 of the transcript. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would submit the credibility of a witness is an important issue for a court to determine. There are matters I would wish to ask this witness, in brief outline, that may affect the credibility of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Given the hour, Mr. Moore, I think we must deal with this tomorrow morning and perhaps, if the witness remained outside tomorrow morning, the issue can be ventilated, Mr. Vasic and you putting your positions, and we will see what the position is. Did you grasp that, Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please ask Mr. Vasic about the witnesses to follow and the respective schedule. I have been planning my own witnesses. If there are no further witnesses to be heard tomorrow, I would like to know what to do next and what about this other witness who has been subpoenaed? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I respectfully reinforce my learned friend, Mr. -- or should I say Judge Borovic's submission in relation to this. And also, we do not know what witnesses are being called by the Radic team and we would be grateful for such pearls of wisdom three days before the event. Secondly with regard to the waivers, I believe the waivers now have been released and we, again, would wish to have a slight conversation with those witnesses prior to them giving evidence so that we can translate those interviews.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will take things one at a time, and I suspect they will simply go on too long for resolution. But the most important and pressing matter, Mr. Vasic, is the question of witnesses for tomorrow and the conclusion of your case.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, Your Honour. Thank you. Much as the last time I addressed this issue, now again I can say, this is our last voluntary witness. We have two witnesses who have been subpoenaed. Mr. Domazet tried to get in touch with one of these over the weekend and I was going to tell you about that tomorrow. As for the other witness, he was finally traced in Belgrade. And it might be helpful, should the Court deem that to be necessary, to have this witness via videolink as well as witness Puskar in relation to whom I would like to submit some medical documents at a time deemed appropriate by the Trial Chamber. Perhaps even outside the case of Mr. Mrksic, outside our own case. Apart from those two witnesses, we have no further witnesses to call. Likewise, the Defence will be filing a motion to tender into evidence certain documents that were not associated with individual witnesses by the Chamber's leave, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, does that mean that you are not in a position to present any further witnesses in your case?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as planned, after Mr. Danilovic we have two witnesses remaining and both are under subpoena. As well as a third witness who suffered a heart attack and who is now in hospital, instead of our courtroom. We shall be requesting a videolink for that particular witness at a later time, whenever it is deemed to be appropriate and feasible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Witnesses may be under subpoena, but if they do not respond and the Chamber has not been persuaded to attempt to take any further steps, well that means they are not available, and you will not be calling them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Things being what they are, we have managed to get in touch with one of these witnesses and I would move that he, too be heard via videolink just like Mr. Puskar, the one in Belgrade. For the other witness, my colleague travelled to Zagreb and could not seem to get in touch with the witness, except via the interphone. And we don't see any other way we could possibly be bringing that witness here, unless other higher authorities step in to resolve this matter. It is now beyond our power. But I would like to be granted an opportunity to make further submissions about this tomorrow, Your Honours. I won't take more than five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do I understand there is no present motion and no arrangements made for a videolink?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have information that this witness has been traced in Belgrade. The first time around we were told that he was not at home, so there was a late phone call to this witness. Last night. As for Mr. Puskar, we are expecting medical documents today and some -- it will take some time after he has been hospitalised for these medical documents to eventually be issued. I ask to have these in the course of the week running, so that we may make appropriate applications for a videolink sometime after we have concluded our case, in relation to these two witnesses, whenever this is most feasible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, it would seem you should plan for next Monday, as indicated when we last discussed this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we are starting on Monday. That was my plan and my schedule. I sent Mr. Moore a seven-day witness plan. Seven names. Seven addresses. Seven days. All the witnesses, according to my schedule at least, so I think I had every right to step in a while ago. I do not wish for this trial to go on endlessly. That at least is what the Radic defence believes. If they have no witnesses, then all of these additional deadlines should not be accepted by anyone. After all, we can't toy around with our witness schedule and we can't toy around with any visas that may be required. That is the principal reason for my previous intervention. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, it seems you ought to have received a witness list from Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We obviously know who the witnesses are but we don't know the sequence of how they're being called. The second matter is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You can discuss that with Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. But what does concern me is the waivers. Now, I understand the waivers have an application to the Court. I understand that fully. But they also have an application to the Defence and the Prosecution. We would like to speak to these witnesses. We tried to do so. The Court knows that I've been to Belgrade. I was unable to do so. And for my part, I would like to set up, please, some method of being able to speak with them because I don't want to delay the Court. So this is a problem we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, I think you stand little prospect of delaying the Court on the issue of whether or not you have been able to speak to these witnesses. It should be able to be resolved between yourself and Mr. Borovic, for you to look at the waivers, if that is the issue you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We will do our best. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. We must now adjourn overtime and we will resume tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I mention one matter. I'm sorry, it's not to do with me and I know Your Honour is exasperated but I have to deal with the topic. Monday is a Jewish holiday. We were hoping that Mr. Weiner would be dealing with the case of Radic. He will be in difficulties if he has to attend on Monday, and we would ask, on his behalf, that the Court does not sit on Monday. His religion, it's Yom Kippur and it creates difficulties for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have some time ago, Mr. Moore, set a timetable. It was suggested bringing it forward to Monday without any issue being raised. That is to next Monday. I can only suggest that for the purposes of Monday, some other counsel will need to be in attendance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would Your Honour consider sitting on Friday, if that was the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That puts an obligation on Mr. Borovic. It is short notice to come forward an extra day. And I don't want, in fairness, to put that obligation on him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I will speak to Mr. Borovic outside about it. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The judges are here, but we've got to try to be fair to both sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
